newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr dumped as rate attraction wears thin.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr dumped as rate attraction wears thin.

text.p: The Australian dollar suffered a second session of steep losses Tuesday as interest rate support over its U.S. counterpart wore perilously thin.

Dealers said contrasting outlooks for U.S. and domestic policy had seen a sea-change in debt markets with some local rates slipping below those in the U.S. As a result the one-year forward rate on the dollar not only moved to a premium, itself a rare event, but reached its highest level in more than a decade.
"Having to pay a premium to buy Aussie forward was a shock to many of my younger colleagues," said one old hand. "I can't remember doing so for any sustained period since 1981."
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the currency was fighting a rearguard action at US$0.7760/65 having fled to US$0.7774/79 at the opening from US$0.7815/20 late Monday and a US$0.7895 peak only last Friday.
Traders said U.S. names had been on both sides of the market with investment banks leading the selling offshore but a big fund providing temporary backing at US$0.7785.

But the bears had the weight advantage and when the fund withdrew there was nothing but fresh air down to US$0.7750. That bulwark held for the remainder of the day, due in part to Asian buying and talk of potential demand related to asset sales.

Dealers have been swapping rumours of a Victorian power station sale for some time and the latest market intelligence was that a deal with a U.S. led group would be announced next week worth anything between A$3.0 and A$5.0 billion.
There were also expectations the sale of three Australian airports would be finalised soon and whispers were they could fetch anything up to A$3.0 billion.

Traders emphasised it was impossible to know how much direct demand for the dollar would stem from these deals -- it would certainly be a lot less than the full amounts -- but the undertainty alone was helping to cushion the currency.
Such support was needed since interest differential were most certainly moving against the local currency when compared to the U.S. dollar.

Dismal domestic employment data last week had set investors thinking about the possibility of another easing here while a horde of robust U.S. indicators had the market pricing in another tightening form the Federal Reserve.

A major result was that one-year Australian money rates had fallen below those in the U.S. and the one-year forward margin, which represents the interest dfferential between the A$ and US$, had climbed to a nine point premium and a multi-year high.

The same contract had stood at a discount of 15 points at the start of the month and reached as low as 41 in February. Indeed, this day last year the forward rate had been at a discount of no less than 170 points.
Bond yields were sharing the same trend and the yield on two-year paper moved below that on Treasuries after standing more than 40 basis points above it a few week ago.
At bottomline this meant investors were no longer paid as much, or in some cases had to pay, to hold Australian dollars instead of U.S. dollars, making the local currency less attractive as a result.
And analysts could see no end to the trend given the U.S. was far more advance in its economic cycle than Australia.

One result was that the inflation outlook here was much more benign, as confirmed by the latest partial price data. Today's figures showed manufacturing input prices fell 0.5 percent in February for an annual drop of 3.8 percent, and followed a modest 0.2 percent rise in output prices reported Monday.
This reinforced expectations Q1 consumer price data next week would show a further slowdown in inflation.
On the crosses, the A$ slid to 97.91/01 yen from 98.59/69 and to 60.3 in trade weighted terms from 60.3. -- Wayne Cole
